The e that is dropped is the e of a split digraph, so children need to recognise split digraph words.
A doubled letter after a short vowel is a pattern children already know from words like rabbit.
Adding -er and -est uses the same base-plus-ending idea as s, -ing and -ed.
-er and -est are added to adjectives, so knowing adjectives helps.
Most jokes and riddles work because a word has two meanings.
Working out what a non-literal phrase or a symbol means is a kind of inference.
A noun group is built by adding adjectives to a noun.
Finding a verb group starts from finding the doing word in a sentence.
Capitals in titles extend capitals for names, and commas are added to sentences children can already mark.
Tracking what a pronoun refers to needs the child to recognise pronouns.
Most contractions join two high-frequency words, so knowing those words helps.
Telling the dog's bone from the dogs builds on knowing that s at the end can mean more than one.
Prepositional phrases extend the everyday phrases for place and time learnt in Kindergarten.
Complex sentences build on joining clauses with and, but and so.
Spoken words keep their own end mark, so children need full stops, question marks and exclamation marks first.
The past tense of regular verbs uses the -ed ending.
Less common vowel patterns are added to the common long vowel spellings already known.
augh and ough in caught and bought spell the same vowel sound as aw and au.
The gh in caught and bought is silent, so knowing silent letters helps.
Choosing between ai and ay by position needs both spellings of the sound first.
Choosing a precise verb needs the child to know the types of verb.
Choosing a precise verb is a case of choosing the best word.
Choosing a conjunction for its meaning builds on knowing how a complex sentence is joined.
An adverb group is built around a single adverb.
Many adverbial phrases are prepositional phrases (in the morning).
Plural possession extends the apostrophe for one owner.
Placing the apostrophe for plural owners needs the plural spelling first.
Using context to choose a meaning builds on knowing that a word can have two meanings.
Working out a word from context is a kind of inference from clues in nearby sentences.
Similes and personification are kinds of figurative language.
Children meet literary devices such as onomatopoeia alongside similes.
These pairs extend the common homophones learnt in Year 3.
Telling its from it's or your from you're needs the child to know what the contraction stands for.
Idioms are non-literal phrases, so children need to know that some phrases are not meant literally.
A pun works only if the reader can hold two meanings of a word in context.
An adjectival clause adds detail to a noun group.
Like a clause after a subordinating conjunction, an adjectival clause cannot stand alone.
Text connectives link sentences in the way conjunctions link clauses.
Connectives often open paragraphs to link one idea to the next.
Keeping tense consistent across a text needs the child to recognise each tense.
Full dialogue punctuation builds on putting quotation marks around spoken words.
The spoken words keep the end mark of their sentence type.
Speech punctuation uses commas, which children first meet in lists.
Persuasive techniques work by presenting opinions as convincing, so children must spot opinions first.
Strong modal words are one of the techniques used to persuade.
Stages of expositions and explanations extend the stages of procedures, recounts and reports.
Each argument stage of an exposition uses persuasive techniques.
The steps of an explanation are a chain of causes and effects.
A metaphor is a comparison without like or as, so children need similes first.
Many idioms are fixed metaphors.
A discussion extends the exposition by setting out more than one side.
Choosing devices for an audience needs the persuasive devices themselves.
Finding the main and dependent clauses builds on the conjunctions that join them.
An expanded noun group often includes an adjectival clause.
The comma marks off an opening adverbial phrase, so children must find the phrase.
Placing commas in dialogue gives practice in using commas to separate parts of a sentence.
Plural and shared possession extend the apostrophe for plural owners.
Irregular plurals such as children take 's, so knowing them helps.
Keeping agreement and keeping tense across a text are checked together when editing.
Changing y to i is another rule for changing a base word before a suffix, like dropping e or doubling.
air and ear are vowel sounds spelt with r, like ar, or and er.
Hyperbole is figurative language, read the same way as metaphors: by what it suggests rather than what it says.
Seeing how a text mixes purposes needs the stages of single-purpose texts, including discussions.
Choosing an emotive word means choosing among words with different shades of meaning.
Emotive words are a key persuasive technique.
